claims.text: Enhanced free-energy sampling during thermal processing enables more precise control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Enhanced sampling can identify key phase-transformation pathways.
Enhanced sampling can identify critical compositional and thermal thresholds.
The relevant initial material is an Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA in an as-cast or solutionized state.
Monte Carlo or other enhanced-sampling strategies can map the alloy's free-energy landscape.
Annealing and cooling protocols can be tailored using transformation pathways identified by free-energy mapping.
Free-energy mapping can determine suitable annealing temperatures and cooling rates.
Phase evolution in the alloy includes stabilization of FCC and BCC constituent phases.
Atomic diffusion and phase-transformation kinetics govern the evolution and stabilization of the constituent phases.
Advanced sampling can quantify free-energy barriers and kinetic pathways in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Knowledge of free-energy barriers and kinetic pathways can guide selection of thermal thresholds that preferentially stabilize desired phases and suppress others.
Sampling-informed thermal treatment will produce a higher proportion of a target phase or a more tailored FCC/BCC ratio than standard thermal treatment.
A tailored phase ratio will improve compositional and microstructural predictability.
Conventional thermal processing produces less predictable and less controllable phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
The complexity and large design space of multi-principal-element systems may limit the effectiveness of the approach.
Uncertainty in simulation predictions under real processing conditions may limit the approach.
The magnitude of improvement in phase selectivity and microstructural retention is not known until experimentally validated.
XRD and SEM/TEM can be used to compare phase fractions and microstructures between sampling-informed and conventional processing groups.
